#8300. The Best Trail Running Shoes for Fall 2026

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

The best trail running shoes boost our confidence on singletrack to scree fields, sand to slick rock. They’re comfortable and nimble and help us run fast or forever, depending on the adventure. As the days grow shorter and colder we’re also looking for shoes that excel under a wide variety of circumstances, like wet leaves, rime ice, and snow. And as the weather deteriorates, we’re also leaning more on road-to-trail models for the days when the roads and paths are calling our names.

Over two to four months of testing on varied terrain across Santa Barbara to Boulder and Nebraska to New Hampshire, our testers Lisa Jhung, Cory Smith, Johnathan Beverly, and Abby Levene provided detailed feedback on fit, comfort, speed, traction, cushioning, and their joy of running. The result is Trail Runner Magazine’s best trail shoes for fall 2026. Considering that the “best” shoe can run differently on someone else’s feet, our review is specially curated with a shoe claiming the title of each chosen category it achieves best. For even more models, check out Outside’s guide to best trail running shoes for fall.

Weight: 7.5 ounces (men’s 8.5), 6.2 ounces (women’s 8) Stack Height: 28.5–21.5 mm Drop: 7 mm Sizing: 7-12.5, 13, 14, 15 (men’s), 6-11 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Responsive and springy + Weightless feeling underfoot + Good ground feel + Excellent traction – Runs small (go half a size up) –Expensive

If the Norda 005 was a car, it would be the Mercedes AMG E63S Wagon. That is to say: it’s quiet performance luxury. IYKYK, as the kids say. Coming in at just 214 grams (7.5 ounces) for a men’s U.S. 8.5, it’s one of the lightest trail running shoes on the market. It’s also made from the highest quality materials: A Biodyneema upper makes it both durable and highly breathable. A slick of Vibram “Megagrip Elite” rubber renders the outsole ultra tacky on the trails while rolling over the roads. And, perhaps most importantly, the midsole is made completely from a proprietary Mouse Arnitel TPEE—a supercritical foam generally only used in small amounts because of the cost—making the shoe featherlight, energetic, and highly durable.

And the simplicity of the design lets the quality shine. As such, it’s a light, fast trail running shoe that can do it all. We’d turn to this shoe for anything from easy days on mixed surfaces, to “fast” trail 100-milers like Western States or Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc. Trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene wore one pair of the Norda 005 for the Tour du Mont Blanc, a five-day, 110-mile adventure through the Alps, and she didn’t think about her feet once. There is no higher praise.

The midsole is tuned to be slightly firmer than the superfoam in road racers and thus provides an energetic, bouncy ride that doesn’t trampoline you in wild directions off the trail. While the lack of a plate may disqualify the Norda 005 from being a true trail “super shoe,” don’t mistake semantics for inferiority. We didn’t miss a carbon plate here, and its absence allows for enhanced ground feel and adaptability to varied terrain. The foam and rocker deliver a smooth roll and plenty of precision.

The only real downside to this shoe is the price tag. But sometimes, you get what you pay for. Read our full review of the Norda 005.

Weight: 9.5 oz (men’s), 8.4 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 32–28 mm Drop: 4 mm Sizing: 7-13, 14, 15 (men’s), 5-12 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Excellent traction + Lightweight and nimble – Slippery laces require double-knotting

We’ve tested every version of the Saucony Peregrine since the model’s debut in 2011, and this sixteenth iteration just might be our all-time favorite. The shoe has long been capable of making us feel nimble on rugged terrain, with its great balance of ground feel and cushioning, plus traction on all kinds of trail, wrapped up in a lightweight package. But version 16 takes the Peregrine’s trail capabilities to new levels, and at $150, it’s an easy pick for Best Value.

The upgraded Vibram Megagrip outsole grips rock slabs with aplomb, while the four-millimeter lugs dig into loose dirt and soft ground (though some sandy-trail testers craved even deeper, toothier lugs). The balanced midsole—not too springy, not too mushy, not too thick—delivers a strong connection to the trail while still feeling responsive and shock absorbing, even during wild descents. The flexible, breathable mesh upper with added toe protection kept out trail debris and warded off snags from roots and branches.

The fit of this trail running shoe somehow made a variety of testers feel like it was custom-made for them. It locks down the heel, and the just-roomy-enough toebox allowed toe space to breathe while maintaining control. “The fit is just perfect,” said a tester. “I feel secure and supported from heel to toe, and side to side.”

Weight: 10 oz (men’s), 9 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 33.5 mm–25.5 mm Drop: 8mm Sizing: 7-13, 14 (men’s), 5-11 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Great traction + Outstanding foothold – Cushioning may feel too firm for some

The Salomon Genesis 2 earned mountain-goat status among our crew, providing outstanding traction over loose dirt and rock. Its supportive Matryx upper—constructed with thin, high-tenacity yarns and durable Kevlar—secures narrow and wide feet alike via Salomon’s quick-pull lacing system. The forefoot offers slightly more room than version 1, enhancing overall comfort without sacrificing agility.

The outsole, made of Salomon’s Contagrip rubber with toothy, 4 mm lugs, provided excellent traction on all surfaces, giving us confidence, even on scrambles over large rocky slabs and slippery descents.

While the EVA-blend midsole runs firm, it offers direct trail feedback. “This shoe makes it fun to pick a line and charge,” noted one tester. “I felt completely present instead of mindlessly rolling over obstacles.”

For technical runners who prefer softer cushioning, we also recommend the La Sportiva Prodigio Pro. (Read our full review of the La Sportiva Prodigio Pro here.)

Weight: 11.7 oz (men’s), 9.5 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 39–31 mm Drop: 8 mm Sizing: 6-15 (men’s), 5-12 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Extremely versatile + Comfortable for all-day wear – Traction could be better

The Nike Trail Pegasus 5 has been our top choice for road-to-trail runs for several seasons, so we were concerned that its newly branded replacement, the Nike ACG Pegasus Trail, would mess with its winning formula. But as soon as we stepped into the new model, we breathed a sigh of relief. The shoe is just as comfortable as its predecessor and, after testing, has proven to be just as capable on and off roads and over gravel, continuing its reign as the most versatile shoe in this roundup.

The midsole foam—Nike’s injection-molded ReactX—feels responsive and cushions comfortably on concrete, pavement, and hard-packed dirt. The outsole traction, from 3.5 mm lugs made of the brand’s proprietary “All Terrain Compound 2.0,” is tackier on wet terrain than the previous version, but still pales in comparison to Vibram MegaGrip.

What makes this shoe work from roads to singletrack trails is the fit and foothold. Even our most narrow-footed testers felt a secure hold without any pressure points, which allows precise footing on trails, no matter how steep or rocky. This shoe’s versatility makes it a great pick as a one-trick pony for the casual runner who doesn’t need a lighter, faster race shoe, and a solid choice for travel.

Weight: 9.5 oz (unisex) Stack Height: 40–34 mm Drop: 6 mm Sizing: 5-12,13 (men’s), 6.5-13.5, 14.5 (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Extremely lightweight for a 40 mm stack + Great stability – Premium pricetag

Brooks has a reputation for building a great shoe and sticking to that formula, giving loyal fans a consistent ride, model after model. The tradeoff? It can make the brand seem boring. The all-new Brooks Cascadia Elite shatters that mold. It’s one of the most exciting shoes Brooks has launched in years, and arguably one of the most exciting trail releases of the year.

Despite sharing a name, the Cascadia Elite is nothing like the everyday, cushioned Cascadia trail runner: It’s a trail racing super shoe that is lighter, faster, and more nimble. The standout feature is the 100% PEBA midsole paired with a carbon-infused PEBAX plate that strikes a perfect balance between a springy and stable ride. On smooth, flowy single track in Santa Barbara, CA, running in the Cascadia Elite felt almost effortless, and a ton of fun.

40 millimeters under the heel is a lot of foam to deal with, but the ride never felt squishy or overly bouncy in off-camber footing. A wide platform, paired with a flexible, embedded horseshoe-shaped plate, keeps the Cascadia Elite from being tippy. That width does come at a cost, though; picking tight lines through technical terrain requires precise footing to keep from getting wedged between rocks.

If you’re in the market for a trail running shoe, first consider the type of trails you run on regularly: do you tackle rugged, mountainous terrain, or stick to mellow dirt paths? Some trail shoes can handle both adequately, while others are specialized and excel in one or the other. Shoes with smaller lugs are generally better on smoother, firmer terrain, whereas shoes with deeper, more aggressive outsoles are optimized for steep, muddy, or rocky trails. If you like to feel the trail and dance around rocks and roots, you’ll likely prefer a light, more minimal shoe, but if you’d rather let the shoe roll over trail variations, cushioning and protecting while you zone out, you should look for a shoe with a thicker midsole.

Once you’ve narrowed the search to a certain type of trail shoe, you need to find a pair that complements your unique body and stride. Every runner’s body, gait, speed, experience, and ride preferences are different, so every runner will interact differently with each trail shoe. The shoe that your best friend or your sister-in-law loves may be uncomfortable for you and make running feel slow, sluggish, or even painful. Finding the perfect pair of trail running shoes is a seriously personal affair.

The process for choosing the best running shoes is a matter of finding the models that both fit your foot and also feel best when you’re running. To determine fit and feel, there’s no substitute for trying the shoes on and running in them.

When assessing fit, first pay attention to length. You need room at the end of your toes as your feet lengthen during their dynamic movements on the run. A rule of thumb is to allow a thumb’s width between your longest toe and the end of the shoe. Runners often wear a running shoe a half or full size bigger than their street shoes.

Ensure that the shape of the sole and the upper matches your foot shape. The sole should be as wide or wider than your foot for the whole length, and match the curve of your arch comfortably. The shoe should hold your foot securely over the instep, while allowing the ball of the foot and the toes to splay and flex when you roll forward onto them. Your heel shouldn’t slip when you lift it, and the arch should be able to dome and lengthen naturally. Nothing should bind or rub as you roll through the stride.

If the shoe fits, it’s time to take them on a short run on a treadmill, around the store, or, ideally, down the block and back. Every trail running shoe has a unique ride created by the type and density of foam in the midsole and the geometry of that foam: its thickness, width, heel-to-toe drop, molded sidewalls or flares, and forefoot flexibility or rocker shape (plus, in an increasing number of models, the presence of and type of embedded plate). Each of these elements interact with each other and your stride to determine how the shoe reacts on landing, how much it cushions, how stably it supports, how smoothly it transitions from landing to toe off, and how quickly and powerfully it rebounds.

The best way to choose trail running shoes that complement your body and stride is to find the ones that feel right on the run. Benno Nigg, the world-leading biomechanics professor who proposed this method of shoe selection, calls it the “comfort filter,” but makes clear it is far more than how plush the shoe feels when you step into it. What you want to assess is whether the shoe allows and supports the way your feet want to move, what Nigg calls your “preferred movement path.” In the right shoe, while running at your normal pace, you will touch down where you expect to land, roll smoothly and stably through the stride without noticing the shoe, feel both cushioned from and connected to the ground, and push off naturally, quickly, and powerfully. When this comes together you’ll know that you’ve found your pair.

It’s likely that several shoes will feel good on your feet. To find the most comfortable, it helps to compare them back to back, like an eye doctor will do with corrective lenses: flipping between “A” or “B,” “1” or “2.” You may also find that different shoes feel better at different paces or level of fatigue, and you may want more than one pair. In fact, research shows that wearing a variety of different shoes is one of the few proven ways to reduce injury risk as it appears to vary the stresses on your feet and joints.

Running shoes have long been marketed and sold as prescriptive devices to help runners stay healthy, but there is little scientific evidence correlating shoes, or any specific shoe properties—like cushioning or pronation control—with running injuries. Medical professionals say that it is highly difficult to determine whether a runner needs a certain type of shoe, and studies have shown that prescribing shoes using traditional methods like treadmill gait analyses or wet-foot arch height tests don’t consistently reduce injuries.

Don’t assume that you need more cushioning or more stability if you have sore joints, or if you’re a heavier runner, or if you’re a beginner—evidence doesn’t support many common beliefs. The best way prevent injury is find two or three different pairs that feel right on the run, ease into using them, and vary your shoes, your running surface and your pace regularly (plus avoid rapid increases in your training load and work on improving your mechanics).

Each season, we evaluate new releases from top outdoor brands, distributing samples to testers based on foot shape and local trail conditions and preferences. For this fall update, we evaluated 5 new models alongside 91 previously tested shoes to select the best trail running shoes on the market.

Over two to four months of testing on varied terrain across the country (from Santa Barbara to Boulder, Nebraska to New Hampshire), our team provided detailed feedback on fit, comfort, traction, cushioning, and responsiveness. We combined these reports with our own trail testing to select category winners and top recommendations for every type of runner.

Freelance journalist, editor, and author Lisa Jhung has researched, tested, and written about running shoes for the past decade and a half, much of that time for Outside. She coordinates a fleet of female shoe testers out of Boulder, Colorado, and says her home office is a perpetual obstacle course of cardboard boxes and piles of running shoes. Lisa’s written about gear of all kinds for numerous national magazines as both an editor and freelancer, including a stint as the shoes and gear blogger and trail running microsite editor for Runner’s World.

A high school jumper and occasional sprinter/hurdler, she started running—really running—after walking off the collegiate volleyball team, and moved on to road and trail races of any distance, triathlons, adventure races, and mountain running. She’s happiest testing rugged trail shoes on gnarly terrain, and also loves a good neighborhood jaunt…but is almost always looking for ribbons of dirt. Lisa is the author of Running That Doesn’t Suck: How to Love Running (Even if You Think You Hate It) and Trailhead: The Dirt on All Things Trail Running.

Cory’s passion for running started over 30 years ago in high school when he became the number six ranked runner in the nation at 3000 meters his senior year. After high school, he competed at Villanova University, earning two NCAA Division I Championship showings. Today, he’s determined not to let age slow him down and competes on the national master’s circuit, running a 4:12 (4:30 mile pace) 1500 meters and 9:04 (4:52 mile pace) 3000 meters in 2021 at age 43. He prefers a hard track workout or tempo run over an easy long run any day but also appreciates a challenging trail or mountain run.

His obsession with running shoes started in 2014 when he wrote his first shoe review for Gear Institute. Since then, he’s tested and reviewed hundreds of running shoes, clothing, and gear for Outside, Runner’s World, Footwear News, and other outlets. He has a soft spot for speedy shoes over heavy trainers but loves dissecting all shoes equally and thinking like a product engineer to explain the why behind every design detail. Cory is the Founder of Run Your Personal Best, an online running coaching business, and since its inception in 2014, has coached runners to over 100 Boston Marathon Qualifying times.

One of Cory Smith’s go-to routes for testing trail running shoes:

Jonathan fell in love with running his freshman year of high school and quickly became fascinated with finding the perfect pair of running shoes. That quest got a boost when he became editor of Running Times in 2000 and started receiving every new model as they were released. The parade of shoes continued while he served as shoe editor for Runner’s World, then editor of PodiumRunner, and currently fitness gear editor at Outside. Having now worn nearly every running shoe created in this century—and a fair amount of those dating back to the early models of the ’70s—he’s given up on finding the one best and now relishes the wide variety of excellent options.

Once a 2:46 marathoner regularly doing 50+ mile weeks, recent injuries and his age have reduced his volume and slowed his pace—but he still enjoys an uptempo workout or two each week. Beverly is the author of the book Your Best Stride which explores how each individual’s gait—and thus shoe preference—is unique. He enjoys getting scientists’ take on new shoe trends and trying to describe the nuances of each shoe’s ride.

#8299. Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Stalking Deer Like a Real Woodsman

Published Nov 19, 2026 4:56 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

The big whitetail buck and I badly startled each other. In the steady rain patter, he apparently didn’t hear me until I’d stillhunted very close to his cedar clump shelter. I almost came unglued when he exploded into view, too spooked to even snort.

After the rifle’s roar shattered the forest stillness, I heard a couple more rhythmic thumps as the by-now invisible deer continued bounding. So much for my semi-frantic snapshot.

But then came a distant, wood-splintering racket, followed by silence. Without snow, it took awhile to slowly, alertly follow up. I found the heart-shot buck. That terminal crash noise came from his failing to clear a windfall when the carburetor quit for keeps.

That’s stillhunting at its best. Unlike the prolonged tedium of trail watching or waiting out a drive, stillhunting’s uptight anticipation is an ongoing thrill. When the action does come, it’s often sudden, without warning. Don’t hunt this way if you have a weak heart.

Very old-timers like my 87-year-old father tell me that forest stillhunting was far more common decades ago. Maybe today’s urban hunters don’t trust their stealth and woodcraft skills. Although not an easy way to take woodland game, including elk, the bottom-line reality is that stillhunting can produce game when other tactics cannot.

Obviously, a lone-wolf hunter can’t make drives to himself. Even when sufficient manpower is available, effective drives require thorough knowledge of both the terrain and how local deer use it. If game chooses not to move because it fed well last night, lacks sexual ambition just now or doesn’t like the prevailing weather, trail watching is usually hopeless. For that matter, many mule deer and most elk and moose simply don’t stick that much to established trails.

The stillhunter is free of such vagaries. Instead of hoping game will come to him, he goes to it — although stillhunting is not the stalking of game already located. Tactically, he has two top priorities. First, to move quietly and alertly, his course basically dictated by wind, terrain and possibly sun direction. Second, to discover game before it sees, hears or smells him. The stillhunter must play a lone-hand game — two hunters seem to make not twice, but four times the noise of one hunter.

Slow movement is a must. A stillhunter covering ground too quickly simply can’t look well enough for concealed game. He also can’t help making extra noise to be picked up by critters who depend on acute hearing every day of their lives to stay out of trouble. They easily detect high frequency noises (including any rustles, squeaks or metallic clinks from our gear and garb) that we often can’t hear.

The real trick in stillhunting is to do the looking and the moving as two separate functions. If you forget everything else, remember that! When you attempt to look for game and move your feet at the same time, sooner or later you will make unwanted noise — snapping a brittle twig, tripping noisily or whatever.

Don’t follow any set rhythm of taking a set number of steps, then stopping. Instead, consider the area that you can see from where you stand as one vision zone. I never move until this zone, of up to 180° ahead and to both sides, has been totally studied.

A vision zone may range out only 50 feet in dense woods or 200-plus yards in more open country. Depending on the extent of the zone, terrain and cover, it may take 30 seconds or several minutes of methodical looking. Often a promising area is worth the time to just sit for extra eyeballing.

Don’t expect to see a full-blown deer or elk looming up ahead like calendar artwork. Look for just parts of the animal as clues. Most forest visuals are vertical lines — tree trunks, etc. An out-of-place horizontal line may be a log or the outline of a deer’s back. A smudge of dull yellow may be autumn leaves or an elk rump. Wide-field binoculars help greatly on such details.

Once, while hunting in the Cascade Mountains, my eye caught a tiny movement ahead. A broad leaf twitching with the breeze? But there was no breeze and, in that evergreen thicket, no deciduous leaves. I waited some minutes, then spotted the movement again for what it was — a blacktail doe’s ear twitching as its owner listened. When she finally moved, right behind her came a shootable buck.

After searching a visual zone (and listening, too), select a route for the next few feet or yards, based on avoidance of brush contact or other potential noise. Footwork is important. Short steps are quietest. They offer best control of shifting your balance if you ease your foot down and feel a twig likely to snap under full weight. Also, only with short steps can you come down slowly and silently on your toes or the ball of your foot. Long steps force the heel down first, making it much more likely that you will snap twigs or make a soft but tell-tale thud.

Want some expert stillhunting lessons? Simply watch a house cat on the prowl for birds or field mice. Slow movement, long look-listen pauses, obvious patience and great concentration are what make felines the finest stillhunters in nature. Once, in Washington’s mountains, I watched a mountain lion on the prowl. This best-of-all deer hunter resembles a magnified house cat at work.

Big or small, hunting cats are superb at using concealment. You should do likewise. Very often, unseen game ahead will hear you. By moving slowly with minimum noise, you may sound much like just another deer. But the listening quarry will be watching in your direction for visual confirmation. Don’t slow yourself any more than necessary. I use camouflage makeup to make my pale face less visible against dark forest backdrop.

If you can move quietly in some kind of concealment, use that route rather than an easier-looking, more open course. Stick to shadows; avoid sunlit patches. When possible, hunt with the sun behind you. Go over ridgetops with caution, using brush or timber cover. If the hilltop lacks cover, try crawling. Of course, stillhunting must be done into the wind or at least across it — never downwind. Although human sense of smell is pretty pathetic, sometimes the barnyard odor of elk ahead can be detected.

Often a stillhunter has the option of following fresh game tracks. Except under ideal conditions, such as new snow, one-man tracking demands so much attention that the stillhunter is distracted while he should be looking for actual game. More than once, deer or elk have surprised me, costing me a shot simply because I was distracted by some interesting tracks. If you start trailing, remember that the maker of these tracks may be bedded down somewhere ahead and almost certainly watching his backtrail. To get anywhere close to it will require extremely good stillhunting.

The lay of the land can be friend or foe. Ridges and hills offer chances to surprise game on the other side. Flat country is tougher because it offers few elevation advantages to the hunter. Although knowing the area always helps, it’s not truly essential for stillhunting. Once, a young stillhunter in our party, new to the place, nailed a whitetail buck the second morning. A fast learner, he capped that next year by pussyfooting close enough to a Cascades bull elk to take him with a bow.

The inexperienced stillhunter is often tempted to work mature evergreen timber, where dense shade means little underbrush. But closely spaced conifers self-prune their branches profusely, forming a noisy layer of dead twigs. Such forests can be hunted only when there’s enough wind noise to cover the hunter’s snap-crackle-pop progress. Unless soggy from rain or wet snow, dead leaves are another audio booby trap.

Some timber is open enough to have a good growth of clover or grass, particularly attractive to elk. By contrast, dense coniferous forests contain little ground-level browse to attract feeding game, but they often provide good escape cover when hunting pressure is on. In unseasonably warm weather, the cool shade of thick evergreen timber invites game. In cold weather, the evergreen canopy traps radiant ground heat for considerably warmer bedding than more open forests.

Where evergreen timber is lacking, game makes the best of thick brushy cover or tall grasses — the latter is commonly a deer favorite. In real cold or after rain, any warming sun draws game to south or west-facing slopes.

Best time of day for stillhunting depends on several factors. Stillhunting as early as light permits may find game feeding or on the move to bedding. Ground litter then is less noisy, thanks to the night’s dampening dew. But if overnight frost has made fallen leaves ultra-brittle or has crusted the snow, better wait for some midday thawing.

Though rain or a moderate wind helps mask hunter movement sounds, strong winds are a mixed blessing. With their hearing impaired by too much wind, restless animals change location often rather than staying put. That aids the stillhunter, because moving game is far easier to see. But wind-jittery animals, up on their feet and watching for danger they can’t hear, can spot the hunter more readily. Fortunately, a stiff wind covers his extra noise if the stillhunter sticks to thicker cover for extra concealment.

Worst of all are those dead-calm Indian summer days, when even your shadow seems to make a racket in the dried-out forest. The only option, then, is to hunt terrain where game can be spotted at a considerable distance (example: from one ridge to another).

Some cover simply can’t be stillhunted. Swampy terrain is impossibly noisy, all the more if there’s any ice to be broken. Dry, fluffy snow can be fairly quiet for walking. But typical autumn snow, heavy and wet, is composed of oversize, many-pointed flakes. Each step compression-shatters untold thousands of such crystalline flakes. That accounts for the appallingly loud squeakiness. Until it’s settled, breaking its flakes in the process, such snow is no good for stillhunting. The settling process may take two or three days unless a thaw speeds it.

Snow characteristics may vary with terrain. North-facing snow is little affected by the weak sun of late autumn, but snow on southern and western slopes settles quickly with a few hours of sun.

The stillhunter must remember that weather affects game’s likely location. The first serious snowfall often causes deer to hole up in the shelter of thick, low-branching evergreens, where they may stay 48 to 72 hours, believe it or not, even during the rut. Hungry when they finally leave cover, deer then are likely to feed during the day. But until they start moving, the pristine snow will be barren of tracks, leading to the false conclusion that all game has moved out.

Of course, game does move out of high country when big snowstorms hit. Hunting deer and elk on such vertical migration routes is often considered a trail-watching game. The stillhunter can cover more territory to learn where game is moving — and if it’s moving.

Gear and clothing are critical in stillhunting. Soft leather boots with crepe soles are almost moccasin-quiet but treacherous in steep, wet or rocky terrain. Classic, Maine-style, rubber shoepacs make quiet steps. Their rounded sole edges are not as likely to shear-snap noisy twigs as stiffer, sharp-edged soles do. With any other rubber footwear, wear enough socks to prevent empty space around the foot from audibly pumping air at each step.

Harder, composition soles with lugs are necessary to maintain life and limb in rough country. Alas, such footwear is noisier. The only consolation is that in country steep enough to require lug-soled boots, the stillhunter has a longer “working range” across canyons, etc., and is not quite as vulnerable to making noise as the close-range, flatland hunter. At times, I’ve carried soft sneakers in my daypack to slip on after climbing a ridge that demanded lug-soled, ankle-supportive boots. Another useful trick is to wear a pair of knit leg warmers running from knee-height to ankles. These muffle twig noise and grass swish.

Clothing choice is very simple. Whatever the material, it must be soft. Nylon, corduroy and stiff denim are too noisy. Wool and flannel are the great favorites for quiet movement. Some synthetics like orlon and acrylic are almost as good, depending on weave and nap. Rubberized raingear makes less noise than nylon or vinyl. Because a hat’s brim snags noisy branches, wear a cap. Again, wool or knitted acrylic is quietest. I made a simple, woolen pack cover to keep my backpack from imitating a snare drum when I hunker through overhanging branches.

For quiet carrying, a firearm’s barrel length is more critical than weight per se. Although carbines are best, one of my favorite woods rifles has a 24-inch barrel. I find a 26-inch barrel is just too easy to bang against branches. A timber riflescope should have at least a 30-foot field at 100 yards — more would be better, because forest shots are often at close-range game on the run. Yellow shooting glasses contrast brown deer and elk better against evergreen backgrounds.

Pocket hardware like keys, coins and cartridges must be handkerchief-wrapped to eliminate tell-tale clinking. When I rendezvoused with my deer-hunting daughter in the woods, her sardonic greeting was, “Hello, Santa!”

“Well before I saw you,” she continued, “I could hear you playing ‘Jingle Bells’. What’s in your pockets?”

A ring of unwrapped keys, that’s what. And deer probably could hear it twice as well as she could.

Although usually not physically taxing, stillhunting is tiring if you do it right. What wears you out is the strain of constant vigilance. And I mean constant! About the time you relax or daydream, up bounds a buck or bull that makes good his escape because you weren’t mentally prepared to react quite fast enough. But if you’re a dedicated hunter, the high-tension hours of stillhunting are memorable whether you score or not.

#8298. Traversing the Saiga Silk Road

As we skidded off the main road and onto a mud path maintained only by tire treads, lines began to blur.

Flanking our two-track trail were a series of parallel lanes no more than a foot wide, which forked, merged, and crisscrossed our own. In the distance, I saw what looked like a ghost train, faintly visible and thrust forward by howling Siberian winds.

Through borrowed binoculars, I soon got my first glimpse of an ancient tableau, seemingly untouched since Neanderthals roamed the earth. On the far horizon, hundreds of nomadic travelers pierced the frigid air with their ringed horns, inhaling the brittle shards through Snuffleupagus snouts as they sprinted across the desolate steppe.

Watching them charge through the treeless plain at full bore, I was reminded of a saying I’d heard shortly before arriving in this remote corner of Kazakhstan: “The saiga is a freedom-loving animal.”

Since time immemorial, saiga antelope have blazed trails across Central Asia while other civilizations rose and fell around them. They once inhabited a world dominated by woolly mammoths, saber-toothed cats, and giant deer with antlers 12 feet across—and outlived them all. When pioneering human caravans first attempted to navigate this unforgiving land, they considered the saigas to be their guides.

Ahead of my arrival, seasonal rains transformed once-green grasslands into sludge punctuated by tufts of withering brush. Driving through such muck is, I would soon discover, akin to controlled hydroplaning. The steering wheel bucked wildly as our tires swerved, shredding deep into the gunk and desperately gripping anything remotely solid enough to push off from.

In the front seats were Alexandr and Albert, two team members from the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan, or ACBK. Between them, they have more than twenty-five years of experience following saigas across the steppe, and I’d arranged to join them for the western leg of one of their field audits.

Our visit was timed to coincide with the rutting season, a critical part of the year for saigas. This is a gathering time, when antelope from across the region sprint together in massive single-file lines, before congregating for a series of competitive battles and subsequent mating rituals.

For males, it’s a time for strutting and headbutting to demonstrate one’s physical prowess to female onlookers—an activity so energy-intensive that many will forget to eat and keel over from extreme physical exhaustion. For females, this is a time of choosing. In addition to assessing fitness, they pay particular attention to one distinctive feature: a potential mate’s floppy, elongated nose. The saigas’ sniffers are essential for filtering out dust in the semidesert plains and for warming frigid winter air before it reaches their lungs. A large nose is the ultimate sign of virility, so as the males marched into these annual gatherings, they were doing everything they could to accentuate their schnozzes.

Because of the saigas’ preference for large-scale migrations across a landscape almost entirely devoid of trees, they have long been a favorite of global wildlife trackers. The isolation and starkness of the saiga world is a strength when it comes to GPS collars, which deliver a reliable stream of daily pings without risk of visual obstruction. Prior to such breakthroughs, conservationists would sometimes spend weeks roaming the boundless steppe unsuccessfully trying to locate the nomadic herds.

The wildlife sanctuary we were traveling through was created only a year prior, with its boundaries informed by tracking data that Albert and his team personally collected. He seemed pleased that the animals were continuing to use the newly designated space as intended. Standing along the roadside, Alexandr spotted a stream of the famously skittish ungulates wrapping around the contours of the earth. As he did, ripping wind and snow started blowing in sideways—the outer ring of an encroaching storm.

These were no fluffy flakes. This was the harsh, crunchy ice of a walk-in freezer, which instantly hardened our truck’s caked-on mud like liquid nitrogen.

Seemingly unperturbed by the dropping barometer, Albert chirped, “Who’s hungry?” Setting up an impromptu picnic, he and Alexandr dug into a prepared meal of fresh bread, tea, and dried meats of unknown provenance. In a muted attempt to thaw my face, I opted to guzzle spicy instant noodles.

A tradition of nomadism has loomed large in this corner of the world since at least the Early Iron Age. The very word kazakh is thought to be derived from the Turkic word qaz, which means “wanderer” or “vagabond.” For millennia, small human groups routinely migrated to higher altitudes in the hot summer months, where melting snow made for abundant water and greenery, before returning to sheltered valleys ahead of winter’s whipping winds. At various times of the year, disparate nomads would also congregate for formal meetings and large cultural festivals, complete with physical challenges like wrestling and tug-of-war. When the gatherings were finished, the nomads dispersed once again.

Historical analysis has shown that nomads’ seasonal migrations and time-honed transit corridors may have helped pave the way for portions of the Great Silk Road, which was less a singular route than an ever-evolving web of pathways and bypasses that linked together reliable stopovers. At the Silk Road’s peak, this corner of western Kazakhstan along the fertile banks of the Ural River became a vital transcontinental crossroads. To this day, the river still serves as a natural boundary between Asia and Europe, meaning this part of Kazakhstan is, quite literally, where East meets West.

The land above the Caspian Sea also served as a main artery that linked together key transit points. Strategic settlements along the riverbank allowed weary caravans to rest their heads, unwind in large public baths, exchange knowledge, stock up on essential supplies, and regroup before moving onward.

Among overland voyagers traversing the continental divide, saigas have long been spoken of with an almost mythical reverence. Cave paintings of the antelope created as far back as the seventh century BCE depict them as resilient, elusive, and charismatic. Expert navigators who embody the true spirit of a most inhospitable terrain.

In human society, traditional nomadic practices persisted even as the land itself was variously claimed and reclaimed by Turkic tribes, Genghis Khan, and the Russian Empire. Only with the rise of the Soviet Union in the twentieth century did mandatory sedentarization efforts successfully manage to lock nomadic people in place, force them to farm, and extinguish a cultural flame that had burned brightly for millennia. Denied the ability to live in perpetual motion, people’s navigational muscles began to atrophy.

This transition was viewed by many as an inevitable shift toward “modernization,” but it also represented a significant diversion from our own history as a species. Of the roughly 300,000 years that Homo sapiens have existed, we spent the first 288,000 of them living in small, mobile groups that followed the migratory patterns of other animals. Forcing nomads into agricultural plots was also a colossal failure because much of the steppe soil was unsuitable for growing crops, which is why so many people were nomadic in the first place. Iconic filmmaker Werner Herzog once remarked that “whatever went wrong and makes our civilization something doomed is the departure from the nomadic life.”

Whether by choice or necessity, most Kazakh people now lead stationary lives in urban centers. The world that nomads once freely roamed has also been feverishly transformed, not only by agriculture but through the construction of new roads and railways.

For the saigas, whose nomadic days never ceased, these new layers now represent an existential threat.

With the weather taking a turn for the worse, Albert and Alexandr ultimately decided to call it a day and start fresh in the morning. After a blistering drive through whiteout conditions, we hunkered down in a tiny village less than 10 miles from the Russian border, where Albert pulled out his laptop and showed me how saiga movements have changed over the years.

“They would routinely trek hundreds of miles as part of an expansive migratory route across the Eurasian steppe,” he said. “Saigas could be found from the Caucasus Mountains to Mongolia, and everywhere in between.”

For millennia, they lived with few barriers and obstructions on the landscape. Then, seemingly overnight, rattling railways and roaring roads began to crisscross the region, fragmenting the saigas into smaller, more isolated groups. As the interior steppe got more accessible to vehicles and passengers, development begat more development.

On his screen, Albert clicked open a recent map that showed how a population of GPS-collared saigas once routinely traveled deep into Uzbekistan before being unceremoniously clipped off by a new rail line in 2014. The data from the years prior to the railway’s construction showed a flurry of squiggly lines representing individual animals zipping back and forth with the seasons. The post-construction slide showed those same animals spinning around despondently on the northern side of the tracks, while the fresh grasses and water they had come to rely on withered away to the south.

Such interruptions can lead to a complete collapse in spatial knowledge—a loss that science writer Ben Goldfarb once wrote is “as thorough as the erasure of a language.” Just as human nomads forced to stay in one place eventually lost connection to the physical landmarks of their ancestors’ journeys, young saigas learn where they can reliably find food and shelter, as well as places to stay away from, through active participation and observation. This cultural exchange keeps their world in orbit and is one of the reasons they have been successful at navigating a terrain fatal to so many before them. As the land they know is cleaved and partitioned, whole stretches of the Saiga Silk Road begin to fade from memory.

To unwind this damage, Albert’s team has partnered with the Kazakh government to construct dozens of saiga-friendly crossing points, where slightly sloping dirt ramps rise up to match the height of the train tracks, making it appear from a distance as though there’s a natural gap in the rail line. Cattle-guard fences positioned far away from the crossings ensure that trains and saigas never actually run into each other at these intersections, which would shatter the illusion of safety.

ACBK has also worked with the Uzbek government to reshape its border fences from a barbed-wire wall to an X-shaped barricade that blocks vehicles from driving through but leaves just enough space for saigas to pass. Over time, Albert hopes such efforts can rebuild the trust necessary for them to confidently return to a plateau they once relied on.

The next morning, I was astonished by how austere the steppe looked compared with the day before. Gone was the slippery muck and browning grasses of shifting seasons, replaced by a blanket of crunchy snow. Against this stark black-and-white backdrop, the fresh crystals functioned like fingerprint dust, illuminating the only remaining pops of color: the rust-red streaks of human and nonhuman pathways in the dirt.

Parked in an otherwise empty tract of prairie land, we watched in stunned silence as thousands of saigas seized the day, flying like banshees across the periphery, their hooves gouging the frozen crust and stamping pigment into an earthen canvas.

As I gazed east toward the colorless horizon, I tried to envision how it might have looked in the thirteenth century, when this corner of the world boasted a vast network of caravanserai, or road inns, where exhausted travelers could rest and recover before continuing onward into the great unknown.

I pondered what it must have felt like for an intrepid merchant to know that they would not see another human being for many days, maybe weeks. To be fearful of what you may soon encounter, but take solace that the space between is not wholly empty. For there is life beyond humanity’s margins, and among nonhuman communities, that in-between space is the center of everything. That, I imagined, must have offered some measure of assurance that the road ahead, perilous though it may be, is well traveled.

This essay was adapted from the new nonfiction travelogue The Hidden Nations of Animals and is published here exclusively for Adventure Journal, with permission from Penguin Random House.

#8296. The Pentagon Wants Public Lands ‘Offered Up’ for a New Army Base. Wyoming Is Interested

Published Nov 19, 2026 6:00 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth wants to build a new military base, and some public land states like Wyoming say they have just the spots.

The base would house between 15,000 and 25,000 active-duty service members, according to a red, white and blue competition flier for what Hegseth is calling the Next Great American Base contest. And ideally it would include 100,000 to 250,000 contiguous acres.

Hegseth said the base should be a “dynamic, self-sustaining power projection platform” with its own power generation, modern air defenses, and advanced technology, reported Newsweek in early October, when the call for pitches first arrived. He went on to say the best proposals would cut through “the red tape, offering up the land and rolling out the red carpet for our military families.”

But much of the “red tape” associated with building a base on hundreds of thousands of acres of unoccupied land is likely federal government red tape. And no clear path currently exists for how to requisition and build a new military installation on federal public land, said Mark Squillace, a natural resources law professor at the University of Colorado Law School.

The Department of Defense would need to work around current Bureau of Land Management or U.S. Forest Service management plans that include stipulations for wildlife like migration corridors and winter range closures.

It’s also unclear if the base needs to support the U.S. Navy, which would limit public-land options since the bulk of the country’s public lands are in the Interior West like Nevada, Idaho and Utah, though the fact sheet says all locations, even those without water access, are on the table.

The DOD already administers 8.4 million acres in the U.S., but is looking to acquire lands managed by other agencies.

Wyoming, for its part, is eyeing both state and federal land for the base. The state’s adjutant general, Maj. Gen. Greg Porter, told a legislative committee in early November that Wyoming has identified at least four “chunks” of state and federal land, as reported by the Cowboy State Daily last week. Which chunks have not yet been disclosed.

Squillace lined out how building a military base on public land could — or could not — become a reality.

The DOD would first likely need to discuss any public land acquisition with the BLM or Forest Service. If the land use agency agrees that a military base would fit the current land management plan, it would need to prepare a draft Environmental Impact Statement that brings up potential complications and confirms compliance with laws like the Endangered Species Act or National Historic Preservation Act.

“A positive review would likely lead to temporary withdrawal of the land from the operation of certain public land laws (like mining and leasing) that could interfere with the operation of the base,” Squillace says, while also noting that existing rights would be protected. Any particularly valuable mining claims would have to be bought out in what he describes as a “time consuming and expensive” process.

Read Next: Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Package that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks

Ultimately, however, Squillace says any large-scale, long-term use of land would likely need to be approved by Congress, “since such transfers of public land are not authorized under law.”  Whether or not the dramatically different Congress to be sworn in next year would green light a public-land transfer requested by Hegseth also remains uncertain.

Christine Peterson is a freelance writer based in southeast Wyoming covering hunting, fishing, outdoor recreation, wildlife and the environment for Outdoor Life, High Country News, National Geographic and others.

#8295. ‘Complete Shock.’ Long-Haul Trucker Hunter Tags 227-Inch Nontypical During State Park Hunt

Updated Nov 19, 2026 6:37 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Indiana’s state park system offers a limited draw hunt that allows residents to target the abundant whitetails on park land that doesn’t get much hunting pressure. There are about 25 parks in the popular program, with two firearms hunts allowed on most of them. Each hunt runs just two days.

“I put in for the early two-day hunt on November 16 and 17 at a Northeast Indiana state park and got drawn for it,” Mike Miltroka tells Outdoor Life. “Trail cameras are not allowed on park [land]. But you can scout before hunt days. I scouted the park on Sunday, the day before the first day of hunting on November 16.”

Miltroka found a likely spot and, well before daybreak on Monday, he was in a tree saddle with his Ruger American Generation II chambered in 7mm PRC.

“It was cool and a little windy, but I was seeing deer soon after daybreak,” says Miltroka, a 38-year-old long-haul truck driver from Farmland. “I spotted a good buck far out, but the cover was too thick to shoot.”

As the morning wore on, Miltroka got a chance to take two does, and he dropped them both with his Ruger. He toted both does to his truck using a deer cart, since motorized vehicles are not allowed off-road.

The spot was already paying off, and Miltroka had a friend — who had seen a giant deer using the area before the hunt — to thank for tipping him off about it.

“I’d never seen the deer previously, but a buddy showed me a video [he’d taken] of the buck a month earlier while visiting the park … It was a place no one else was hunting, and I checked to make sure it was okay to hunt there – and it was.”

On the second day of the hunt, Miltroka chose a different tree. He climbed into a big walnut closer to the cover where he’d seen the buck on Monday. But unlike the day before, Miltroka didn’t see much except a coyote. Then, around 8:30, things changed.

“I heard something raking trees behind me, and I didn’t know what it was. I kept trying to see what was making all that racket, then I saw him out about 70 yards,” he says. “I knew it was a good shooter buck, and when I got him in my scope I squeezed the trigger, fired, and the deer took off running.”

Miltroka jacked another round into the chamber, but as soon as he picked up the running buck in his scope again, the deer went down.

It wasn’t until Miltroka studied the dead buck through his scope that he realized how immense the deer was.

“I started shaking, and yelling,” he says. “I got buck fever after it was over … I called a friend of mine and was so excited he asked if I was tied tight to my tree, and I said yes. I was shaking so much I might have fallen out of it.”

Once he was steady enough, Miltroka climbed down and walked up on the deer.

“I was in complete shock,” he says. “I’ve only taken about six bucks, and none even have the size of this one. I was screaming with joy.”

He filled out a transport tag for his buck, which filled his limit of three deer for the park hunt – only one of which can be a buck. Then he wheeled the buck to his vehicle, loaded it, and drove to park headquarters to check it in.

The buck’s field dressed weight was 181 pounds. The 22-point nontypical was green scored by an official Boone & Crockett measurer the day after Miltroka shot it. It gross scored 227 inches, with a net score of 197 6/8s inches. It has an outside antler spread of nearly 25 inches, and one main beam of the rack measures over 27 inches.

He will have the buck scored again after the required 60-day drying period for B&C and will enter the buck into B&C’s nontypical record category. He’ll also submit his buck to the Hoosier Record Buck Program.

“The park hunts are well run and there are plenty of deer,” says Miltroka. “I saw lots of deer being checked in during the hunts and some nice bucks.

Read Next: ‘Over the Moon.’ Ohio Hunter Shoots 215-Inch Buck from Her Favorite Stand on Her Birthday

“I’m stunned at the size of my deer. But there are so many great bucks that have come from Indiana.”

A correction was made on Nov. 19, 2025: A previous version of this article included photos from a different 200-plus inch buck the author is reporting on. It has been updated with the correct deer and deer hunter.

#8294. The Ephemeral Global Climbing School Amid China’s Epic Limestone

On October 22, hundreds of climbers of all skill levels descended upon Yangshuo, China, for the long-awaited  2026 Arc’teryx Climb Academy. Participants say the remarkable thing about the weekend wasn’t just the climbing or even the new skills they learned—it was the magic of the remote, fantastical landscape, and the opportunity to connect with people across cultures and continents.

The Arc’teryx Climb Academy is a roving international climbing school—and one that offers some of the most advanced mountain education in the world. Since 2007, academies have been held in global climbing epicenters like Squamish, Chamonix, and Mammoth Lakes. Some focus on climbing while others offer backcountry or freeride skiing education. Each installment is a complex undertaking, bringing together world-class guides and athletes to pass on their knowledge in a highly efficient, structured format. Dozens of courses—ranging from alpine overnights to big wall workshops to mental resilience clinics—are designed to meet participants where they’re at. At each academy, students can learn skills from scratch, drill fundamentals, or significantly boost their skills, even within just a few days of instruction.

While there are tons of events in the climbing universe, Arc’teryx Climb Academies stand out for just how seamlessly they’re run and how well integrated they are into the local community. Unlike some climbing festivals, which tend to put more emphasis on socialization than education, Arc’teryx has figured out how to nail both without compromising either. All day long, participants of every skill level take hands-on courses on some of the best rock in the world, each one packed with pro-level hacks, technique drills, and actionable tips for continuing your education after the trip ends. Each evening, a five-star lineup of films, speakers, music, and parties makes it impossible to tear yourself away. Every chapter of the event buoys you along to the next. The weekend passes in a flash. And you return home with more phone numbers, more new climbing partners, and more stoke than you could have imagined possible.

In 2023, the series brought this special blend of inspiration and education to the limestone cliffs of Yangshuo, China—and the event was a runaway hit. In 2024, the Academy returned with even more courses crafted specifically for the local community, including rescue and evacuation clinics tailored to China’s uniquely rocky landscapes. The 2026 Academy further expanded the course menu, offering beginner trad clinics, bolting workshops, and masterclasses in big wall climbing. Over four days, hundreds of climbers participated in 37 clinics at more than a dozen crags across the stunning Guangxi region. It was the region’s biggest Arc’teryx Climb Academy yet.

While many of the Academy’s participants came specifically to experience Yangshuo’s world-renowned karst spires, the crags aren’t just a backdrop here; they’re the heart of a thriving and longstanding community of climbers, route developers, and outdoor businesses. Since international climbers first arrived in the late 1980s, the zone has grown to nearly 2,000 routes across 74 crags on world-class limestone.

“Yangshuo means a lot to me,” says Peng Zhou, renowned Chinese mountaineer and Arc’teryx athlete. “I completed both my first 5.12 and 5.14 routes here, and it has left me with many wonderful memories.” He loves getting an opportunity to share this place with newcomers; it’s one of the reasons he comes back to teach year after year.

Given Yangshuo’s robust existing climbing scene, the event offers more cultural exchange than top-down discourse. Here, international visitors learn just as much from their Chinese counterparts as locals learn from the global pros.

Take it from Arc’teryx athlete Quentin Roberts. This year, he taught his third Yangshuo Big Wall Climbing clinic in a row. Each time, he’s astonished by how much the climbing community has grown since his last visit. “Every year I feel like I have had to level up to meet the growing ambitions and skills of the participants,” he says. “It’s exciting to see how eager everyone is.”

But for Roberts, the best part about climbing in China is the profound and indescribable warmth of the Yangshuo community.

“We always have a big, Chinese-style, round-table dinner with all the instructors before the event,” he says. It’s an evening filled with laughter between old friends. Jokes and stories fly across the table like sparks, and Roberts leaves feeling filled up at a soul level. “Many of the people in that room are at the forefront of climbing in China. It’s special to feel that sense of family, and to see the passion everyone has for what they’re doing.”

It’s that sense of connection that makes the Yangshuo event—and the other installments of the Arc’teryx Climb Academy—so invaluable.

“Coming to China over the years and connecting with people through climbing has really reinforced something I believe deeply: we are all more similar than we are different,” says Roberts. “Climbing has an incredible ability to bring people together. Sharing a rope, trusting one another, sharing our experiences—those connections transcend language and culture.”

Arc’teryx is a Canadian company based in the Coast Mountains. Our design process is connected to the real world, focused on delivering unrivaled durability and performance in extreme conditions. Our products are distributed through over 160 branded stores and more than 2,400 retail locations worldwide. We are problem solvers, evolving and searching for a better way to deliver resolved, minimalist designs. Good design that matters makes lives better.

#8293. Level Up Your Next Family Ski Trip at Banff Sunshine Village

Sunshine Ski Village in Banff, Canada. (Photo: Sunshine Ski Village)

One of the best things about skiing with kids is that your definition of a great day changes. It stops being about vertical feet, powder depth, or how many black diamonds you can check off before lunch. Instead, it’s about finding a mountain where everyone can have fun together today while still having room to grow tomorrow.

That’s what makes Banff Sunshine Village such a gem for families. What really sets this ski destination apart is the balance between beginner, intermediate, advanced, and expert terrain. Skiers of all levels have plenty of runs to explore, making it easy for families of mixed abilities to spend the day on the mountain together. Across three connected mountains and more than 3,500 acres of terrain, there’s room to return season after season as confidence grows and skills evolve.

For many families, the sweet spot starts on the lower mountain around the Wolverine and Jackrabbit chairs. These areas feel like they were designed by people who know what it’s like to ski with enthusiastic kids. Runs like Miss Gratz, Rollercoaster, Kids Play, Wolverine, and Blue Bell offer the perfect mix of gentle pitches, playful rollers, natural features, and kid-approved tree skiing. Instead of simply sliding down groomers, young skiers and riders get to explore terrain that quietly teaches balance, turning, and confidence while they’re busy having fun.

That natural terrain approach creates a progression that feels effortless. One season you have your kids between your own skis, the next they’re asking to duck into the trees or tackle steeper lines.

As abilities advance, Sunshine keeps delivering. Families ready to explore more challenging terrain can tap into Banff Sunshine’s Ski & Snowboard School, where lessons help skiers and riders build confidence well beyond the beginner stage. For those interested in freeride skills, specialized instruction and the resort’s beacon training area provide a chance to learn mountain safety fundamentals in a controlled environment before taking on bigger adventures.

The secret weapon might be staying slopeside at the Sunshine Mountain Lodge. Instead of ending the day with a drive back to town, families can stretch the adventure into the evening. Tobogganing, movie nights, hot tub bingo, and nightly s’mores give kids something to look forward to after the lifts stop spinning, while parents get a chance to relax and enjoy being fully immersed in mountain life.

The best family ski destinations aren’t the ones you outgrow. They’re the ones that grow with you. At Banff Sunshine, that’s exactly what happens.

Banff Sunshine Village is the premier ski and snowboard resort in the Canadian Rockies. It’s famed for being home of Canada’s Best Snow – light, fluffy, smoke-dry powder and for having the longest non-glacier season in Canada. The resort is typically open from early November until late May. Guests of Sunshine can elevate their Canadian Rocky Mountain experience by staying at Sunshine Mountain Lodge, the Banff National Park’s only ski in, ski out hotel.

#8292. The Rules of Trail Running Etiquette, from the ATRA President

As the president of the American Trail Running Association (ATRA)—a title that sounds more impressive than it is—and co-author of The Ultimate Guide to Trail Running,” which is now in its third edition, I know a little about the proper behavior of trail runners. And as a six-decade trail veteran myself, I also know a little about the improper behavior of trail runners.

To me, the “rules” of trail running are quite simple and boil down to two principles: respect nature, and respect other users.

Those two tenets blossom into about 10 “strong suggestions” for sustainable, copasetic trail experiences, but, like with the Golden Rule, it all comes down to showing respect. Here are the basics of what you should know when you hit the trails:

Close any gates you open, don’t disturb the wildlife or livestock, and respect private land and get permission to enter.

Take only photos and pack out at least as much as you brought in, including gel wrappers. If needed, wear shorts, a jacket, or hydration pack with zip pockets to stow rubbish found on the trail.

Don’t disturb wildlife as frightened animals may be dangerous. Steer clear of trails that disturb sensitive habitats during nesting or mating seasons. When passing horses, use special care and follow directions from the horseback riders. Consider turning around and going another direction when faced with large herds of animals.

Don’t play your music loudly, engage in boisterous conversations with your fellow runners (or through speakerphone), or listen to headphones so loudly that you are unaware of your surroundings. Along the same lines, do your social media influencing elsewhere. Nature is not your recording studio. We don’t want to hear you, and you ought to be able to hear others.

We expect the same of cyclists. This should be obvious but, then again, all of this should be.

As trail runners, we move relatively quickly, especially when we seemingly emerge from nowhere on unsuspecting trail users. This may be alarming, so anticipate and give a courteous and audible announcement of your presence and intention to pass hikers on the trail by stating something along the lines of, “On your left,” or “Trail,” as you approach. Keep an eye out for those wearing headphones, as they won’t hear your warning. Be courteous when passing, slowing down or stopping if necessary to prevent accidental contact. Be ready to yield to all other trail users (cyclists, hikers, horses) even if you have the posted right of way.

This is likely to be controversial, but consider not bringing your dog on group runs and, when you do run with your dogs, be sure to leash them and keep them under your control when necessary to prevent any wildlife disturbances. Be sure to pack out their (and your) waste.

Be cognizant that off-leash dogs often chase wildlife and degrade the outdoor experience of other trail users.

Greet and say “Excuse me” to those you see and pass on the trail. This should be a common practice if for no other reason than to alert others to your presence and not frighten anyone. Similarly, be sure to stay in control of your speed, especially when you could cause rocks or other trail features to fall.

If you startle someone, apologize, and thank them if they’ve stepped aside. A little kindness goes a long way on the trail.

Don’t cut the switchbacks or widen trails by running around puddles,downed trees, or when it is too muddy

Don’t create your own trails by running off preexisting, well-marked trails. When multiple trails exist, run on the most worn. Stay off closed trails and obey all postings.

Run single file in the middle of a trail, even if it’s laden with a fresh blanket of snow or thick mud. Go over, not around, obstacles like puddles,rocks, or downed tree limbs, as that widens trails, damages vegetation, and causes unnecessary erosion.

In other words, participate in trail maintenance and give back to the trail community.

In a now-infamous Outside opinion piece of seven years ago that went viral, Marc Peruzzi claimed that trail runners are lazy parasites. Ultrarunner and lawyer Stephanie Case wrote a response piece, saying more could be done, agreeing with my stance that “we are guilty as charged … we need [to do] more. A lot more.” Case continued, “Indeed, as trail running continues to increase in popularity, it will become even more important that we expand our volunteer and conservation efforts.”

So, carry your weight and do trail work. Volunteer. Go plogging on your local trails.

Technically, those ascending are supposed to have the right of way but, in practice, people often yield to descenders, likely due to speed and momentum. Be polite, maintain control, and be prepared to yield to other users, including horseback riders.

Split larger groups into smaller groups as bigger numbers can intimidate other users and have a greater environmental impact on trails.

If you come across someone in distress, stop and check whether they need help.

Don’t become a liability by taking risks, getting lost, or ignoring trail closures that require dangerous rescues. Carry proper clothing, nutrition, and hydration so as not to put yourself at risk of exposure. Safety first is always a good rule.

If running alone, familiarize yourself with the area where you plan to run and let at least one other person know your intended route. Be prepared for the weather and conditions when you start your run and plan for the worst, given the likely duration of your run. Know and respect your limits and report unsafe conditions and activities to the proper authorities.

Trail running is beautifully simple. So is being a courteous trail runner. Follow these tips for proper etiquette and keep the trails safe, welcoming, and wild!

While we don’t always find the best selection of climbing gear at REI, the co-op is currently staging its big Holiday Sale, which lasts through November 23. There are some great steals for climbers in the mix, from a dry rope we love, to a solid shoe pick.

Currently, REI members can also take 20% off one full-price item, so check out our gear guides if there’s a new or full-price piece of gear you have your eye on. You can find our latest rock climbing gear guides (updated this fall) here, as well as our newest winter gear guide here. REI doesn’t have all of our top picks in stock, but you may be able to score on some of our favorites this season.

Below are a few of our favorite climbing deals on climbing shoes, ropes, purpose-built pants, and more gear that our editors and testers love.

While not a top pick in our recent shoe guide, we reviewed the Katana Lace in 2024 and called it an excellent shoe for edging and precision placements. It’s also great in narrow cracks and pockets. This is a good first performance shoe for the climber starting to think more about progression, and a great shoe for a climber who cares about performance, but doesn’t want an insanely uncomfortable pair to push their absolute limits. I’ve been climbing in the Katana since last winter and have found it a joy to wear in hand cracks, finger cracks, steep routes, and technical climbs with edging in the gym and on all types of rock. It’s not so great as a comfortable, all-day pair on moderates, or for slab, in my opinion.

Our favorite rope for trad climbing (as of fall 2026), the Black Diamond 9.4mm dry rope balances durability, sleekness, and light weight. During our testing process, we took big whippers, found ourselves hangdogging on steel permadraws, didn’t obsess over the dirt that got into our rope, and ran the 9.4 over grainy lips on sport pitches and across arêtes and edges on mixed and traditional pitches, as well. After months of testing, the rope barely showed any wear, which is notable for a 9.4 that feels skinny in hand and climbs as smooth and airy as an ultra-light—great for rope drag on monster sport climbs or zigzagging trad leads.

At the time of publication, only the 70m was in stock, with low inventory. If you’re climbing in low-moisture areas, you could get the same rope without the dry treatment (also 20% off), or save 20% on the 9.6mm version if you don’t mind the larger diameter (this version is a bit pricier because it’s bipatterned, making it easier to find the middle—worth the premium, in our opinion).

Our best all-around harness of fall 2026, the Black Diamond Solution uses what it calls Contour Edge Technology for the waist and leg loops, meaning they’re more rigid in the middle, but flexible and soft at the edges for increased comfort. Our testers loved the contoured hip support and the durability of this harness. “I took hundreds of falls and [the Black Diamond Solution Guide] gets the highest praise I can give a harness, which is that I never even thought about my harness after a fall,” one of our testers said.

Our top all-around men’s climbing pant of 2025, Black Diamond’s Alpine Light Pants feature a mobility-friendly design. We also selected them as our top women’s pick for trad climbing, multi-pitch routes, and alpine lines. While the Alpine Light pants are out of stock or low inventory right now, the Black Diamond Alpine Pants (which are, as you might expect, a bit less lightweight) are currently on sale. We found that this pant model struck an ideal balance between breathability while moving quickly, and moderately protective in light winds and rain showers with its DWR coating.

One of our top mountaineering boots of the year, the G-Summit climbing boot accomplishes a small but significant miracle: It’s a double boot that climbs like a single boot. The insulated foam liner—combined with the wrap-around inner shell and external gaiter—creates an envelope that’s warm enough for high-altitude mountaineering, and yet low-profile and precise enough for hard technical climbing up to WI6 and M7. The rubber rand was sticky enough to provide purchase in foot jams on B.C.’s Stanley Headwall, and the Vibram sole gave testers enough grip to cross boulder fields and icy scruff in Norway, Patagonia, and beyond.
